title: Monitoring the Internal Monologue: Probe Trajectories Reveal Reasoning Dynamics
claim: Monitoring hidden-state probe trajectories and their signal features reveals behavior that surface-level reasoning text hides when it is unfaithful.
layout: 3 panels: pipeline strip on top, bar chart bottom-left, trajectory plot bottom-right
description: The figure has three panels. Panel (b) is a rounded pipeline strip across the top. A Prompt box leads into a Reasoning Process container. Inside it, a gray box shows the generated CoT text, labeled as possibly unfaithful. Below it, a yellow box shows hidden representations h1…hN, which feed a blue Probe Trajectory box. That box leads to a green box listing the signal features to extract (global statistical state, shape and trend dynamics, temporal segmentation). An arrow then leads to a Future Behavior box. Panel (a), bottom-left, is a grouped bar chart of the percentage of CoT that is faithful for seven base models on WildGuard (dark blue) and Aegis (green). Panel (c), bottom-right, plots probe score against percent of tokens, with four colored mean trajectories over faint individual traces. Dashed boxes with magnifier icons mark regions of interest. A smaller delta-score plot sits underneath.
caption: Overview of the trajectory-based framework. (a) Surface-level CoT is unfaithful to the final output in $3%$ to $12%$ of cases, depending on model and dataset, necessitating latent monitoring to ensure safety. (b) Our framework monitors hidden representations to generate probe trajectories, from which we extract signal features (e.g., statistical state and trend dynamics). (c) These features capture dynamics that distinguish behaviors even when the CoT is unfaithful. Notably, the extracted signal features make it easier to differentiate between unfaithful cases: those with a safe response and unsafe CoT (violet line) and those with an unsafe response and safe CoT (orange line).
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) introduce new opportunities for safety monitoring through their Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, CoT is not always faithful to the model's final output, undermining its reliability as a monitoring tool. To address this, we investigate the hidden representations of LRMs to determine whether future behavior can be predicted from prompt and CoT representations. By evaluating a probe at each generated token, we construct a probe trajectory, the continuous evolution of a concept's probability across the reasoning process. To characterize these temporal dynamics, we extract signal-processing features that capture volatility, trend, and steady-state behavior. We find that trajectory features help precisely where the static probe is weakest, adding 21.7 AUROC points on average, and improving in every such case where that probe falls below 70. We also present two methodological insights. First, template-based training data achieves near-parity with dynamically generated model responses, eliminating the need for a costly initial inference and labeling. Second, the use of a pooling operation is necessary: last-token methods achieve poor performance, whereas average and max pooling achieve 78.5% to 97.4% AUROC and yield stable probe trajectories. Across seven reasoning models from three families and six evaluation datasets, we find probe trajectories to be a promising signal for monitoring model behavior.
